about: Reference list /gramatica/verbos-com-preposicoes (Portuguese: verbs with prepositions). items: [verb + preposition, what follows (alguém = somebody, algo = something, inf. = infinitive), example, level]. Sorted by preposition; a section's name is the preposition itself (the worksheet and the live quiz blank it in the example, so each example must use it as the verb's preposition before any other use of the same word, and no other preposition of this list may also be right in that gap). Examples avoid contractions (do, na, ao) so the bare preposition stays visible.

ptBR.note: Brazil often uses ir para / chegar em / entrar em where Portugal says ir a / chegar a / entrar em; assistir a also means “to watch” there.

title: Verbs with prepositions
metaTitle: Portuguese verbs with prepositions: list with examples – Reference – icanspeak Portuguese
description: Common European Portuguese verbs with a fixed preposition, sorted by a, com, de, em, para and por: what follows each one, and an example sentence.
lead: The most common verbs with a fixed preposition, sorted by preposition. For each verb: what follows it and an example.
regel: Learn the verb and its preposition together: *pensar em, sonhar com, depender de.*
After a preposition, a verb stays in the infinitive: *Sonho com ter uma casa perto do mar.*
In questions the preposition goes first: *Com quem falas? Em que pensas?*

Some verbs take no preposition in Portuguese where English has one: *procurar as chaves* (look for), *ouvir rádio* (listen to), *pagar a conta* (pay for), *esperar o autocarro* (wait for; *esperar por* also works).
*a, de, em, por* join with the article: *ao, do, no, pelo.* *Falo do problema. Penso na família.*
In Portugal you go *a* a place you visit (*vou a Lisboa*) and *para* a place you go to stay or live (*vou para o Porto viver*).
practice: Pronouns after prepositions: para mim, comigo
